issues.legal_issue: A defendant’s absence from the country is excluded when computing the limitation period for a civil suit.
material_facts: The suit sought specific performance of an agreement to sell and was filed after the ordinary three-year period from the possible accrual dates of the cause of action.

The defendant was in the country only during limited intervals between the accrual of the cause of action and the filing of the suit; the remaining period of absence, if excluded, made the suit timely.
issues.conclusion: The defendant’s periods of absence from the country had to be excluded, and the suit was within time.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(5) of the Limitation Act, 1963, corresponding to Section 13 of the Limitation Act, 1908, requires exclusion of the time during which the defendant was absent from India. The rule applies whether the cause of action arose in India or abroad, and whether the defendant was in India or abroad when it arose. The Court relied on P.C.K. Muthia Chettiar v. V.E.S. Shanmugham Chettiar, which considered Atul Kristo Bose v. Lyon & Co. and Muthukanni Mudaliar v. Andappa Pillai.

predicates.civil_suit_subject_to_limitation: The claimant brought a civil suit that was subject to a limitation period.
predicates.defendant_absent_from_country_during_lim: The defendant was outside the country during part of the period in which the claim could be brought.
predicates.absence_period_covers_excess_delay: Excluding the defendant’s absence from the calculation leaves enough time for the suit to have been filed within the applicable limitation period.

issues.definition: When a civil suit subject to limitation is filed after a period partly covered by the defendant’s absence, the suit is timely if excluding that absence covers the excess delay.

issues.legal_issue: Business efficacy cannot be used to imply a contractual term that changes a clear and deliberate allocation of payment obligations.
material_facts: The agreement required the buyer, at the seller’s request, to pay amounts for the seller’s tax dues directly to the tax authorities, up to the remaining sale consideration.
The agreement did not require the buyer to pay any further amount directly to the seller or into the seller’s bank account after the initial payment.
The seller sought a further payment directly to him or into his bank account to enable him to provide a bank guarantee.
issues.conclusion: The agreement did not require the buyer to make the further payment directly to the seller, and the High Court was not justified in implying such a term by applying business efficacy.
issues.legal_principle: A term may be implied for business efficacy only if it is necessary to give the contract its intended effect and was clearly intended by the parties; a court may not imply a term merely because it seems reasonable. The Court relied on The Moorcock, United India Insurance Company Ltd. v. Manubhai Dharamasinhbhai Gajera, and the observations in Shirlaw v. Southern Foundries and Trollope and Colls Ltd. v. North West Metropolitan Regional Hospital Board.

rule.if: contract_dispute and contract_language_clear and payment_recipient_specified and proposed_term_changes_payment_recipient

predicates.contract_dispute: The parties disputed the meaning or effect of a contract.
predicates.contract_language_clear: The contractual language clearly stated the parties’ relevant obligations.
predicates.payment_recipient_specified: The contract identified the person or authority to whom the relevant payment had to be made.
predicates.proposed_term_changes_payment_recipient: A party sought to imply a term that would require payment to a different recipient from the one specified in the contract.

issues.definition: If a contract dispute concerns clear language that specifies a payment recipient, a court does not imply a term changing that recipient.

issues.legal_issue: A buyer is ready and willing to perform, and the seller is in breach, when the buyer offers payment in the manner required by the agreement but the seller insists on a different manner of payment.
material_facts: The buyer stated in correspondence that he remained ready to pay any requested amount, within the agreed limit, to the tax authorities as the agreement required.
The seller’s demand for a further amount was made directly to the buyer, and the seller did not establish that he had requested payment to the tax authorities under the agreement.
The seller did not proceed with the sale, while the buyer continued to seek completion of the transaction.
issues.conclusion: The buyer was ready and willing to perform his part of the contract, and the seller defaulted by insisting on payment in a manner not required by the agreement.
issues.legal_principle: Readiness and willingness are assessed from the claimant’s overall conduct before and after suit, considered in light of the other party’s conduct; no fixed formula applies. The Court relied on J.P. Builders v. A. Ramadas Rao and the earlier decisions R.C. Chandiok v. Chuni Lal Sabharwal, N.P. Thirugnanam v. Dr. R. Jagan Mohan Rao, and P. D’Souza v. Shondrilo Naidu.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.buyer_offered_contractual_payment: The buyer offered to make payment in the manner and to the recipient specified in the agreement.
predicates.seller_demanded_different_payment_recipi: The seller insisted that the buyer make payment to a recipient different from the one specified in the agreement.
predicates.seller_made_no_contractual_request_to_au: The seller did not request that the buyer make the payment to the authority identified in the agreement.

issues.definition: In a specific performance suit, a buyer who offers contractual payment is ready and willing, and the seller is in breach, when the seller demands a different payment recipient without making the contractual request to the specified authority.

issues.legal_issue: A long delay and substantial increase in property value do not, by themselves, bar specific performance where the claimant was not responsible for the delay and maintained a live interest in enforcing the agreement; the court may require performance at the current market value.
material_facts: More than forty years had passed since the agreement, and the value of the property had greatly increased.
The plaintiffs were not responsible for the delay and had participated in the proceedings, showing a continuing interest in enforcement.
The seller was in breach, and the Court had no material before it to determine the property’s current market value.
issues.conclusion: The Court decreed specific performance, directing that the sale be for the property’s market price as of the date of its order, with the trial judge to determine that price.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963, the discretion to grant specific performance depends on the facts and must be exercised on fair, reasonable, and rational principles. Delay and escalation in property prices, by themselves, are not valid grounds to refuse relief, though they may justify requiring a higher price or additional compensation. The Court relied on P.S. Ranganath Reddy v. M.K. Bhagyalakshmi and Narinderjit Singh v. North Star Estate Promoters Ltd.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and seller_in_breach and claimant_not_responsible_for_delay and claimant_maintained_live_interest and substantial_property_value_increase

predicates.specific_performance_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.seller_in_breach: The seller failed to perform the seller’s obligations under the agreement.
predicates.claimant_not_responsible_for_delay: The claimant did not cause the delay in obtaining a final decision.
predicates.claimant_maintained_live_interest: The claimant continued to pursue enforcement of the agreement through the proceedings.
predicates.substantial_property_value_increase: The property’s value substantially increased during the delay.

issues.definition: When a seller is in breach and a claimant in a specific performance suit did not cause the delay, continued to pursue enforcement, and faced a substantial increase in property value, specific performance may be granted at current market value.
